notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0096.stoa004.opp-la: Line 2: the edition marks a gap with asterisks (* *), given here as [...]. Line 8: 'fni' is read as fui. The Marsi were proverbial as snake-charmers and enchanters, so 'a Marsian' means a sorcerer. In line 13, (one) is the editor's addition.

Commodian's Latin is irregular and the passage seems corrupt in places. Line 388, 'canentibus rostra elusissent', is obscure and rendered literally; 'those who sang' are presumably the prophets. In line 390 'seruus ipsa' is read as seruitus ipsa, 'slavery itself'; in line 394 'erint' is taken as erunt. 'They' who call him a magician are those who rejected Christ, apparently the Jews.

nodes.text: THE APOLOGETIC POEM OF COMMODIAN.
Who will be able properly to know the one God of the heavens,
except one whom he has carried [...] away from abominable error?
I wandered, roaming in ignorance, captive to an empty hope,
while the frenzy of my early years bore me into the air.
I was lighter than chaff; as if there were a hundred
heads on my shoulders, so headlong was I carried wherever [it took me].
That was not enough: by these doings, in the end, a criminal Marsian
I was almost made, chanting spells over malignant herbs.
But thanks to the Lord (and my voice is not enough to give back
so much), who at last shone on me, wretched and tottering!
And I set to work on the handed-down book of the Law,
[to learn] what I might find out there; at once a lamp shone for me.
Then indeed I recognised God, (one,) highest in the heights,
and therefore I urge such people to withdraw from error.
when that people which is referred to already rejoices in him?
But those wretches, who dress up empty tales
and defame [him] as a magician, had mocked the mouths of those who sang.
What shall I call them? Before they had been scattered,
they whom neither exile broke nor slavery itself.
If he had been a magician, why then did the prophets sing
that he would come from heaven, so that he himself would be the hope of the nations?
If they declared falsely of them that they would lose their land,
which has come to pass for them, so too the things about him will be false.
But because they have always been spurned, since they were bloodthirsty,
they rebel against their own Lord, calling him a magician.
Nor do they want to hear what the prophets said against them,
